edits.body_md: This is White Nights, a poignant tale of love, loneliness, and dreams, written by Fyodor Dostoyevsky, translated by Tim Zengerink, narrated by Zeke Ring.

### The Poetic Heart of a Lonely Dreamer

White Nights is one of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's most lyrical and tender works, a short story that captures the fragile beauty of human connection and the aching poignancy of solitude. First published in 1848, early in Dostoyevsky's career, it belongs to a period before his more mature philosophical and psychological novels such as Crime and Punishment or The Brothers Karamazov. Yet, despite its brevity and relative simplicity, White Nights contains emotional and thematic depths that have made it one of his most beloved and enduring stories.

Set in the magical twilight of a St. Petersburg summer, when the sun never fully sets and the nights are awash in a surreal silvery light, the story follows a solitary, unnamed narrator, a dreamer who wanders the empty streets at night. He lives more in his imagination than in the real world, finding comfort in fantasies and silent buildings, in poetry and ideas. But his quiet, repetitive life is interrupted when he meets Nastenka, a young woman weeping on a bench.

Over the course of four nights and one morning, they share a brief, intense intimacy that changes them both. The story is not just a romantic interlude. It is an exploration of the human need to be seen, to be heard, to be loved. It is about the yearning for connection in a world that often feels cold and distant. Dostoyevsky, who himself was prone to melancholy and isolation, gives voice here to a character who longs not for glory or wealth, but simply for a moment of understanding.

Through the dreamer's confession, the reader is drawn into a soul that feels deeply and asks for very little, but finds that even a little can be everything. Unlike many of Dostoyevsky's later characters, who are torn by guilt, ideology, and inner chaos, the narrator of White Nights is gentle, kind, and almost painfully innocent. He is a man untouched by cruelty, yet marked by the pain of being invisible.

His love for Nastenka is pure and unselfish, rooted not in desire but in a deep emotional bond. And that is what makes the story so moving. It is not about possession or fulfillment. It is about giving without expecting, loving without demanding, hoping even in the face of certain loss.

### Light, Shadows, and the Ephemeral Nature of Love

The setting of White Nights is more than just a backdrop.

It is a vital part of the story's emotional atmosphere. The White Nights of St. Petersburg. Petersburg, those luminous summer evenings where night never fully arrives, mirror the dreamer's emotional state, a space between darkness and light, between sleep and waking, between fantasy and reality. It is a time when ordinary life is suspended and something otherworldly seems possible. This luminous unreality is what makes the dreamer's encounter with Nastenka feel so enchanted.

They meet not in daylight, where the world imposes its rules and expectations, but in this in-between space where hearts speak more freely. For four nights, they walk and talk, sharing their hopes and sorrows. The dreamer opens up in ways he never has before. He is not trying to impress or manipulate. He simply wants to be close to someone. Nastenka, too, is lonely and vulnerable. She tells him of her strict grandmother, her confined life, and the man she loves who promised to return but has not.

Their connection is real, but fragile. They understand one another, yet they are not meant to last. The dreamer falls in love with Nastenka, but she is still in love with someone else. When her former lover returns, she goes to him, and the dreamer is left alone once more. But Dostoyevsky does not present this as a tragedy. There is sadness, yes, but also beauty. The dreamer has had his moment.

He was seen. He was needed. He was loved, even if briefly. And for someone who has lived in the shadows, that is no small thing. His final words are not bitter, but full of gratitude. A whole moment of happiness. Is that too little for the whole of a man's life? This line captures the spirit of White Nights. It is a story about fleeting joy, not because it is destined to vanish, but because its very ephemerality gives it meaning.

The dreamer is not destroyed by disappointment. He returns to his solitude, but something in him has changed. He has touched another soul. He has known the light. This emotional nuance is part of what makes White Nights resonate so powerfully. In a world where love is often portrayed as dramatic, possessive, or transactional, Dostoyevsky offers a vision of love that is quiet, selfless, and tender. A love that expects nothing and gives everything.

A love that, though brief, illuminates a life.

### The Dreamer, the Outsider, and the Seeds of Dostoyevsky's Themes

White Nights is not just a love story. It is a portrait of the dreamer as an outsider. The narrator lives on the margins of life, observing others, constructing imaginary relationships, and yearning for a reality he cannot enter. He is not mentally ill, nor is he a social rebel. He is simply alone, painfully aware of his isolation, and yet he maintains a hopeful, even childlike heart.

This figure of the dreamer would evolve in Dostoyevsky's later works into more complex, conflicted characters. Raskolnikov, the underground man, Prince Mishkin, Ivan Karamazov, all share with the dreamer a sense of dislocation, a struggle between inner vision and outer reality. But in White Nights, the dreamer is still innocent. He has not yet been hardened by suffering or drawn into philosophical rebellion. He still believes in the possibility of love, kindness, and simple human connection.

What makes this story so valuable, especially within Dostoyevsky's larger body of work, is its emotional purity. It shows the author in a more tender mode, unburdened by religious or political weight. There is no murder, no confession, no courtroom, no philosophical duel, just two people walking through twilight, trying to make sense of their hearts. And yet, the themes that would come to define Dostoyevsky's writing are already present.

The search for meaning, the pain of being unseen, the dignity of suffering, the paradox of joy and sadness coexisting. Even the idea of redemption, not through ideology or punishment, but through human connection, is here in its earliest, gentlest form. The form of the story, first-person narration, framed as a confession or letter to the reader, also anticipates Dostoyevsky's later narrative techniques. The reader becomes a witness, not just to events, but to emotion.

We are not told what to think or feel. We are invited to listen, to empathize, to imagine ourselves in the dreamer's shoes. White Nights also has a universal quality that transcends time and culture. Anyone who has ever felt invisible, who has longed for connection, who has experienced a brief, unforgettable love, will find themselves in these pages. It is a story about moments, about how the smallest encounter can echo through a lifetime, about how the heart, even when broken, can remain soft.

As you begin reading White Nights, let yourself be drawn into its quiet world. Feel the stillness of the city, the glow of the sky, the hesitations and confessions of the characters. Let the story move slowly. It is not meant to shock or thrill. It is meant to make you feel gently, honestly, deeply. Welcome to White Nights, a tale for the lonely, the hopeful, the dreamers. A soft whisper in a sleepless night, a reminder that even the briefest connection can light up the soul.

Half my story you know already, that is, you know I have an old grandmother. If the other half is as brief as that, I interrupted laughing, be quiet and listen. First of all, you must promise not to interrupt me, or else I might lose track of what I'm saying and end up all muddled, so listen quietly, will you? I have an old grandmother. She's been my guardian ever since I was a little girl, because my father and mother both passed away when I was very young.

Grandmother must have been better off financially in the past, for she often recalls the good old days. She's fond of talking about how things were when she was younger, about the elegance of society, the way people behaved, and how different everything is now. She taught me French herself at first, then hired a teacher for me when I got a little older. When I was fifteen, and now I'm seventeen, so it wasn't so long ago, we stopped the lessons altogether.

That was around the time when I began getting into mischief. I won't tell you exactly what I did, because really it wasn't anything serious, but it was enough to upset grandmother. One morning she called me to her side and said that because she was blind and couldn't keep an eye on me, she had to take drastic measures. She took a pin, yes, a real pin, and fastened my dress to hers.

Then she declared that we would sit like that for the rest of our lives unless I started behaving better. Can you imagine? Sitting there, tied to her, day after day? At first there was no escaping her. I had to work, read, and study right beside her. I wasn't even allowed to take a step away without her permission. I did try to outsmart her once. I persuaded Fekla, our charwoman, to sit in my place while grandmother was napping.

Fekla is deaf and doesn't hear much of anything. Grandmother was dozing in her armchair, so I thought everything would be fine. I slipped away to visit a friend who lived nearby, thinking I'd be back before she even noticed. But of course it didn't go as planned. Grandmother woke up while I was gone and started asking questions. She thought I was still sitting there quietly next to her.

Poor Fekla didn't know what to do. She couldn't understand what grandmother was saying and panicked. In her confusion, she undid the pin and ran off. At this point, Nastenka burst out laughing, the memory clearly amusing her. Her laughter was infectious and I couldn't help but laugh with her, but she stopped almost immediately and gave me a warning look. I'm serious. Don't you dare laugh at grandmother. I'm only laughing because it was funny and—well, what can I do?

That's just how grandmother is. But I'm fond of her in my own way. Oh, how I caught it that time, though. As soon as I came back, she pinned me right back in place, and after that there was no sneaking off again. I wasn't allowed to stir an inch. Oh, I almost forgot to tell you. Our house belongs to us, or, rather, it belongs to grandmother. It's a small wooden house with three windows, as old as grandmother herself.

There's also a tiny upper story. Recently a new lodger moved into the upstairs rooms. Then you must have had an old lodger before, I commented casually. Of course we did, Nastenka replied with a hint of exasperation, and let me tell you, he knew how to keep quiet better than you do. In fact, he hardly spoke at all. He was a frail, dried-up little old man, deaf, blind, and lame.

He was so feeble that eventually he just couldn't go on living anymore. He passed away, and after that we had to find someone new to rent the room. We can't manage without a lodger. The rent, along with grandmother's pension, is nearly all we have to live on. But this time the new lodger wasn't an old man. He was young, a stranger, not from around here. Grandmother took him in because he didn't haggle over the rent.

It was only after he moved in that she asked me, Nastenka, tell me, what's this lodger of ours like? Is he young or old? I didn't want to lie to her, so I told her the truth. Well, grandmother, I said, he isn't exactly young, but he's not old either. And is he pleasant-looking, she asked? I didn't see any point in lying about that either. Yes, grandmother, I said, he's pleasant-looking.

Oh, what a nuisance, grandmother exclaimed. What a nuisance! I tell you, Nastenka, you'd better not get any ideas about him. Times are so different now. Why even a lodger like this? And he has to be pleasant-looking, too. It wasn't like this in the old days. Grandmother was always reminiscing about the old days, how everything was better back then. In the old days, she would say, she was young and full of energy, the sun was warmer, the flowers bloomed more brightly, and even the cream didn't turn sour so quickly.

Everything, it seemed, was perfect in the old days. Whenever she started talking like this, I would sit quietly, holding my tongue, listening patiently while she lamented the present and glorified the past. But in my mind I couldn't help but wonder why she had even brought up the lodger's looks in the first place. Why did she suggest it to me? Why did she ask whether he was young and good-looking?

But that was all I did. I wondered for a moment, then I put the thought out of my mind. I counted the stitches on my knitting, focused on my work, and forgot about the lodger entirely. Life carried on as usual. One morning, however, the lodger came into our room. He had come to ask Grandmother about her promise to have his rooms repapered. The conversation started about wallpaper, but soon drifted to other topics.

Grandmother, being naturally talkative, kept the conversation going. At one point she said, "Nastenka, go into my bedroom and bring me my reckoner." I jumped up immediately, eager to fetch it for her, but in my hurry I completely forgot that my dress was still pinned to hers. I blushed furiously, not knowing why, and instead of quietly undoing the pin so that the lodger wouldn't notice, I leapt up so quickly that Grandmother's chair shifted.

The lodger's eyes widened slightly, and in that instant he realized the full extent of my predicament. When it dawned on me that he now knew everything, that he understood the ridiculous situation I was in, I froze. I stood as still as a statue, unable to move, my face burning with embarrassment. And then, to my utter horror, I felt tears welling up in my eyes. I didn't know where to look, didn't know what to do.

Grandmother, unaware of what was happening, called out again, "What are you waiting for?" But her words only made things worse. The tears began falling freely, and I was completely overcome with shame and misery. I felt as though I would sink into the floor if I could. The lodger, seeing how distraught I was, must have felt sorry for me. Without a word he gave a polite bow and left the room quietly.

His kindness only deepened my embarrassment. After that, I became terrified of hearing the slightest sound in the hallway. Every creak or shuffle of footsteps made my heart race, and I would immediately think, "It's him, the lodger!" I would frantically undo the pin, just in case I needed to escape quickly, but it never was him. Day after day passed, and he didn't come back. A whole fortnight went by without any sign of him.

Then one day he sent a message through Fekla. He told her he had a large collection of French books, good, worthwhile books, and that I might like to borrow them so I wouldn't get bored. He added that Grandmother might approve of this, and he hoped it would help pass the time. When Fekla delivered the message, Grandmother, as always, was cautious. She accepted his kind offer with gratitude, but immediately began asking questions.

"Are the books moral?" she asked. "Because if they're not moral, then it's out of the question. You mustn't read anything improper, Nastenka. People learn terrible things from such books." "What terrible things, Grandmother?" I asked. "What could possibly be in them?" "Oh, plenty," Grandmother said gravely. "These books are full of stories about how young men seduce innocent, virtuous girls. They pretend to love them, promise to marry them, and then whisk them away from their parents' homes, but once they've ruined the poor girls' reputations, they abandon them, leaving them to suffer the most pitiful fates." "I've read many books like that myself," she added, almost as an afterthought, "and I must say, they're written so vividly that you can't help but stay up all night reading them.

Of course, I read them on the sly," she admitted with a sly little smile. "But you, Nastenka, mustn't read such things. What books has he sent you, anyway?" "They're all Walter Scott novels, Grandmother," I replied. "Walter Scott's novels?" she repeated thoughtfully. "Well, those sound proper enough. But wait, are you sure he hasn't hidden anything inside them? These young men can be crafty. Have you checked to see if there's a love letter tucked inside the pages?" "No, Grandmother, there's no love letter," I assured her.

"Hmm," she said, unconvinced, "have you looked under the binding? Sometimes they slip things under the binding, those rascals." "No, Grandmother," I said again, "there's nothing under the binding." "Well, then," she finally conceded, "if you're sure, that's all right." So we began reading Walter Scott, and within a month or so we had made our way through almost half of the novels he'd sent us. Then more books began to arrive.

He sent us Pushkin as well, and soon enough I couldn't imagine my days without a book. I left behind my childish daydreams of marrying a Chinese prince, for now the stories I read filled my mind with far richer and more vivid fantasies. That's how things were when one day, quite by chance, I encountered our lodger on the stairs. Grandmother had sent me to fetch something, and I was hurrying down when I saw him coming up.

As we passed, he stopped, and for a moment neither of us spoke. I blushed, he blushed. Then he broke the silence with a friendly laugh, greeted me with a cheerful, "Good morning," and asked how Grandmother was doing. "Well," he added, "have you been reading the books I sent?" I nodded and said that I had. "Which ones did you like best?" he asked. "Ivanhoe," I answered, "and Pushkin, most of all." That was the extent of our conversation that time.

I hurried away, feeling both shy and strangely pleased, while he continued on his way upstairs. A week later I ran into him again, this time in much the same place. Only this time Grandmother hadn't sent me on an errand. I had gone downstairs of my own accord to fetch something. It was just past two, and I knew from habit that this was the hour he usually returned home.

"Good afternoon," he said, as he stopped on the stairs. "Good afternoon," I replied, trying to keep my voice steady. "Aren't you bored?" he asked, "sitting with your Grandmother all day long?" When he said this, I felt an immediate rush of embarrassment. I didn't know why. Perhaps it was because I felt as though he had touched on a sensitive subject, one that others had already whispered about. It wasn't the first time someone had hinted that my life was dull or limited, and though I didn't like hearing it, I couldn't deny there was truth in the question.

I felt both ashamed and offended, but I also found myself rooted to the spot, unable to walk away. "Listen," he said gently, "you're a good girl. Forgive me for speaking so directly, but I truly want what's best for you, just as much as your Grandmother does. Don't you have any friends you could visit, someone to talk to or spend time with?" I told him the truth.

"I don't have any friends now," I said. "I used to have one, Mashenka, but she moved away to Pskov." "I see," he said thoughtfully. Then, after a pause, he added, "Would you like to go to the theatre with me sometime?" "The theatre?" I repeated, startled. "But what about Grandmother?" "You'd have to go without telling her," he said with a quiet smile. "No," I said firmly, "I don't want to deceive Grandmother.

Good-bye." "Good-bye," he replied, and though he said nothing more, there was something in his voice that lingered with me, even after he was gone. Later that day, after dinner, he came to see us in our little sitting room. He stayed for quite a while talking to Grandmother about this and that, asking her questions about her life and habits. At one point he casually asked if she ever went out, if she had acquaintances or places she liked to visit.

Grandmother shook her head, laughing, and said she was too old for such things now. Then, quite suddenly, he said, "I've taken a box at the opera for tonight. They're performing The Barber of Seville. My friends were supposed to join me, but they've cancelled, and now the ticket is going to waste." "The Barber of Seville!" Grandmother exclaimed, her face lighting up with interest. "Why, that's the very same one they performed in the old days." "Yes," he said with a smile, glancing briefly at me.

"It's the same barber." I could feel my face burning. I knew what he meant by that glance, and my heart began pounding in suspense. I kept my eyes on the floor, not daring to look up. But I could feel Grandmother's excitement growing. "To think of it," she said, "I once played Rosina myself in a private performance. That was many, many years ago." "Then perhaps you'd like to go to-night," the lodger suggested.

"It would be a shame for the ticket to go unused." "By all means, let's go," Grandmother declared with enthusiasm. "Why shouldn't we? And besides, my Nastenka here has never been to the theatre in her life." My goodness, what joy! As soon as the plan was decided, we began getting ready, without delay. Grandmother and I put on our very best clothes. Even though she couldn't see, she was eager to hear the music, and I could tell she was just as excited as I was, though for a different reason.

She was a kind and selfless soul, my Grandmother, and what mattered most to her was that I had the chance to enjoy myself. She would never have gone to the theatre on her own, but knowing it would bring me happiness she agreed without hesitation. As for me, I could hardly contain my excitement. The anticipation alone was thrilling. When we finally arrived at the theatre and took our seats, I could scarcely focus on anything around me.

The lights, the crowd, the atmosphere, it was all so overwhelming and magical. What my impressions of the Barber of Seville were, I won't even attempt to describe. The music, the performance, the characters, it felt like I had stepped into an entirely new world. But what stood out even more to me that evening was the way our lodger behaved. He looked at me so kindly, spoke so warmly, that it was impossible to mistake his intentions.

I realized then that his suggestion that morning, that I should go to the theatre with him alone, had been a test, a way of gauging my character, and knowing that made me feel proud, like I had passed some unspoken challenge. That night, as I lay in bed, I was brimming with happiness. My heart was beating so fast that I thought I might have a fever. I couldn't stop thinking about the performance, replaying every moment of it in my mind.

All night long I dreamed of the Barber of Seville, and when I woke the next morning it felt as though I were still under its spell. Naturally, I expected that after such a delightful evening, the lodger would start visiting us more often. But to my disappointment, that wasn't what happened at all. He seemed to grow even more distant. He only came by about once a month, and even then it was only to invite us to the theatre again.

We went twice more, but by then my joy had started to wane. I began to feel that he didn't truly care for me, that his kindness was only out of pity for my situation. He saw how strictly Grandmother treated me, and that was the extent of his feelings, sympathy, nothing more. As time passed, I grew restless. I couldn't focus on anything, not my reading, not my knitting, not even my conversations with Grandmother.

Some days I found myself laughing uncontrollably, doing silly things just to provoke a reaction from her. Other days I would break down in tears for no apparent reason. My emotions were all over the place, and I couldn't make sense of them. I began to lose weight and felt constantly on edge, as though something inside me was about to break. When the opera season ended, the lodger stopped coming to see us entirely.

The only times I saw him were by chance, on the stairs. Each time he would bow silently, gravely, as if trying to avoid any unnecessary interaction. He would continue on his way, and I would stand there, rooted to the spot, my face burning red with embarrassment, my heart pounding as though it might burst. Then came the end. It was exactly a year ago, in May, when the lodger came to us with the news.

He told Grandmother that his business in Petersburg was finished, and that he would be returning to Moscow for a year. As soon as I heard those words, I felt the ground shift beneath me. My legs gave out, and I sank into a chair, barely able to breathe. Grandmother of course noticed nothing. She simply listened politely as he explained his plans, and when he finished, he bowed and left the room.

I was devastated. What was I to do? I thought and thought, turning everything over in my mind, but nothing made sense. I felt trapped, helpless, as though my world were collapsing around me. Finally, I made up my mind. The next day, he was to leave, and I resolved to take action that very evening, after Grandmother had gone to bed. So it happened. I gathered all my clothes, packed the linen I would need, and tied everything into a bundle.

With the parcel in hand, I climbed the stairs to his room, more dead than alive. My heart was pounding so violently that I thought I might faint. I stood outside his door for what felt like an eternity, unable to summon the courage to knock. When I finally opened the door and stepped inside, he turned to look at me. His face went pale, and he cried out in shock.

He thought I was a ghost. Rushing to my side, he fetched a glass of water, for I could barely stand. My head was spinning, and I felt as though I were about to collapse. When I finally recovered enough to speak, I placed my parcel on his bed, sat down beside it, and buried my face in my hands. Tears poured from my eyes in a torrent, and I couldn't stop myself.

I cried as though my heart were breaking, and in a way it was. I think he understood everything in that moment. He didn't need me to explain. He looked at me with such sadness, such quiet regret, that it tore at my heart even more. Listen, he said gently. Listen, Nastenka. I can't do anything. I am a poor man. I have nothing, not even a proper job. How could we live if I were to marry you?

We talked for a long time. I poured my heart out, telling him that I couldn't bear living with Grandmother any longer, that I felt like I was suffocating, that I would rather run away than go on like this. I even said that I would follow him to Moscow if only he would let me. Shame, pride, and love were all swirling within me, clashing and fighting for control.

At last, I collapsed onto the bed, overcome with emotion, trembling with fear at the thought of his refusal. He sat in silence for several minutes. Then, at last, he stood, walked over to me, and took my hand. Listen, my dear, good Nastenka. Listen to me, he said, his voice soft yet filled with urgency. I swear to you that if I am ever in a position to marry, you will be the one to make me happy.

I assure you truly that right now you are the only person who could bring joy into my life. But listen, Nastenka, I must go to Moscow. I'll be there for a year, and during that time I hope to improve my circumstances, to establish myself properly. When I return, if you still love me, I swear to you that we will be happy. I will make sure of it, but right now it's impossible.

I simply can't do it. I don't have the means, nor do I have the right to make any promises I might not be able to keep. Still, I repeat, if it doesn't happen within a year, it will certainly happen at some point. That is, of course, only if you don't prefer someone else during that time. I could never ask you to bind yourself to me with any sort of promise, and I wouldn't dare try.

I want you to be free to choose. That was what he said to me, and the very next day he left for Moscow. We agreed between us not to say a word to grandmother. That was his idea, his wish, and so the matter was left as it was. Well, she continued, her voice softening with a mixture of sadness and resignation, that's almost the end of my story.

A whole year has passed now. He has come back. He's been in Petersburg for three days already, and—and—and what? I interrupted eagerly, unable to contain my impatience. What happened? Has he come to see you? And up to now he hasn't shown himself, she answered, summoning all her courage to get the words out. Her voice trembled, and it seemed as though even saying it aloud caused her pain.

There's been no sign, no word from him. She stopped there, as though the weight of her emotions had become too much to bear. For a moment she sat still, her head bowed. Then, suddenly, she buried her face in her hands and broke into such uncontrollable sobs that it sent a pang straight through my heart. I hadn't expected this. I had thought her story would end differently, more happily.

The sight of her despair was almost too much for me to bear. Nastenka, I began timidly, trying to keep my voice gentle and soothing. Nastenka, please don't cry. How can you be so sure? Maybe he hasn't arrived yet. Perhaps there's been a delay. No, no, he's here. He's already here, she interrupted, her voice choked with tears. I know he is. We made an agreement that evening before he left.

We agreed on everything. We came here, to this very embankment, after we talked that night. It was ten o'clock, and we sat on this bench. I wasn't crying then. I felt so hopeful, so happy to hear everything he said, and he told me that as soon as he arrived back in Petersburg, he would come to see me. He said that if I didn't refuse him, then we would tell grandmother everything.

But now he's here, and he hasn't come, he hasn't come, and I don't understand why. She broke into tears again, her shoulders shaking as she tried to stifle her sobs. Good God, Nastenka! There must be something I can do to help, I exclaimed, jumping up from the bench in sheer desperation. Tell me, tell me, Nastenka, wouldn't it be possible for me to go to him, to speak to him on your behalf?

Could you really do that, she asked suddenly, raising her head and looking at me with a glimmer of hope in her tear-filled eyes. No, no, I said, quickly pulling myself back to reality. Of course not, it's impossible. But I'll tell you what, you could write him a letter. A letter, she repeated, shaking her head as her hope faded. No, that's impossible, I can't do that. But why not, I insisted, clinging to my idea.

Why can't you write him a letter? It depends on the letter, Nastenka. There are ways to write such letters. Trust me, please, trust me, I wouldn't give you bad advice. It can be done. You've already taken the first step once. Why not now? I can't, she said firmly, lowering her head again. I just can't. It would feel as though I were forcing myself on him. Ah, my dear, sweet Nastenka, I said, barely able to hide a small smile.

No, no, you have every right to reach out to him. Think about it. He made you a promise. He told you that if he married anyone it would be you. He even gave you the freedom to refuse him, didn't he? That shows he's a man of delicate feeling, someone who cares about doing what's right. Under the circumstances, you have every right to take the first step. In fact, you're in a privileged position.

You can even free him from his promise if you feel it's necessary. I paused, letting my words sink in. Don't you see, Nastenka? You have nothing to lose and everything to gain. Listen, how would you write it? she asked suddenly, her voice trembling slightly with a mix of uncertainty and determination. Write what? I asked, though I already had an idea of what she meant. This letter, she clarified, looking at me with wide expectant eyes.

I hesitated for a moment, then nodded. I'll tell you how I'd write it. Begin with, Dear Sir. Must I really start it like that? she interrupted, frowning slightly. Dear Sir? Is that how it should begin? Yes, you certainly must, I replied with confidence, though almost immediately I wavered. Though after all, I'm not entirely sure. Perhaps it depends. Maybe you could start differently if you feel it suits you better.

Well, well, go on, she urged, leaning forward eagerly. What comes next? Dear Sir, I began again, trying to compose the rest of the letter in my mind. I must apologize for—no, wait, that doesn't seem right. There's no need to apologize. The very fact that you're writing justifies itself. Apologies would only weaken the point. Write simply, plainly, like this. I am writing to you, forgive me my impatience, but I have lived a whole year in hope, and that hope has sustained me.

Am I to blame if I cannot bear even a single day of doubt now that you are here? If by any chance your feelings have changed, this letter is not to reproach you or to plead. It is only to tell you that I do not hold you responsible, nor do I blame you. How could I, when I have no power over your heart? Such is my fate.

I know you to be an honorable man. You will not ridicule or grow angry over these lines, written in such haste and emotion. Please remember that they come from a poor girl who is entirely alone, who has no one to guide her or advise her, and who has always struggled to control her heart. If a shadow of doubt has crept into my heart, forgive me for it.

I know you are not capable of offending, even in thought, someone who has loved you so deeply and continues to love you still. I stopped and glanced at her. Nastenka's face had lit up with joy, her eyes sparkling with excitement. She clapped her hands together and exclaimed, Yes, yes, that's exactly what I was thinking. Oh, you've solved everything for me. God has truly sent you to me.

Thank you, thank you. I couldn't help but smile at her enthusiasm. Thank me? What for? For God sending me your way? I asked, half teasing, but entirely delighted by the happiness in her expression. Yes, for that too, she replied with a playful laugh, her cheeks glowing with warmth. Ah, Nastenka, I said, my voice softening. There are moments in life when one feels grateful simply for existing at the same time as someone else.

I thank you, not just for meeting me, but for giving me something I'll remember for the rest of my life. She smiled at that, but quickly waved her hand as though brushing away my words. Enough, enough of that. Listen now. Let me tell you what we agreed upon that night before he left. We decided that as soon as he returned, he would let me know by leaving a letter with some good, trustworthy people I know, people who know nothing of the situation.

Or if writing a letter was impossible, since letters can't always say everything, he promised to meet me here, at this very spot, at ten o'clock on the day he arrived. I know he's already back, I feel it. But now it's been three days and there's still no sign of him, no letter, no message, nothing. And it's impossible for me to leave grandmother alone in the mornings. So please, here's what I need you to do.

Take my letter to those kind people I mentioned. They'll send it on to him. If he replies, bring his answer here tomorrow at ten o'clock. I hesitated for a moment, thinking through the logistics of her request. But the letter—I said—you have to write the letter first. That might delay things, so, perhaps, everything will have to wait until the day after tomorrow. The letter—Nastenka repeated, her voice faltering slightly as a flicker of uncertainty crossed her face.

She looked down, fiddling nervously with her hands. The letter— But— She trailed off, leaving her thoughts unfinished. But she didn't finish her sentence. Instead, she quickly turned her face away from me, her cheeks flushing the deepest pink, as though a rose had bloomed upon her skin. For a moment she hesitated, and then, without a word, I felt something soft pressed into my hand. Looking down, I realized it was a letter—sealed, prepared, and clearly written long before.

She must have carried it with her all this time, ready for this moment, though perhaps unsure whether she would have the courage to hand it over. As I stood there, a familiar, sweet memory swept over me. A thought that seemed as if it had sprung to life from some tender corner of my imagination surfaced unbidden. I couldn't help myself. With a mischievous grin I began softly, R-O-R-O-S-I-C-N-A-N-A.

Rosina! we both burst out together, humming the name in unison. The laughter that followed seemed to fill the quiet street, mingling with the soft evening air. In my delight I came close to embracing her, swept up in the shared joy of that silly little moment. Her laughter mixed with mine, though her cheeks grew even redder and tears glistened at the corners of her eyes. They sparkled like tiny pearls against the dark curtain of her eyelashes, catching the faint light.

"'Enough, enough! Stop it now!' she exclaimed, half laughing and half scolding, though her own voice betrayed her amusement. "'Good-bye for now,' she added hastily, as though trying to end the moment before her emotions got the better of her again. "'Here's the letter. Take it. And here's the address where you're to deliver it. Don't forget. Good-bye, till we meet again. Till tomorrow.' Her words tumbled out so quickly that I hardly had time to respond.

Before I could say anything more, she pressed both my hands in hers with a warmth and sincerity that left me momentarily stunned. Her grip was firm, but her hands trembled slightly, as though she were both eager and afraid of what would come next. She gave me one last bright, fleeting smile, nodded her head quickly as if to reassure herself, and then turned and darted away. She moved so quickly, so gracefully, that she seemed almost to fly.

Like an arrow loosed from a bow, she vanished down the side street, her footsteps light and quick against the cobblestones. I stood there, rooted to the spot, unable to move, watching her retreating figure as it disappeared into the shadows. Even after she was gone, her voice lingered in my ears. "'Till tomorrow. Till tomorrow.' The words echoed, their warmth wrapping around me like a melody that refused to fade.

I stood there for what felt like an eternity, staring at the empty street where she had just been, my heart full of something indescribable. And then, at last, I turned and began to make my way home, her letter clutched tightly in my hand.

Today has been a dreary, rain-soaked day, one without even the faintest trace of sunlight. It's as though the sky itself is reflecting the gloom in my heart, the weight of thoughts pressing down on me like the clouds above. The rain feels endless like the old age that stretches out before me, colorless and joyless. My mind is restless, swarming with strange, unanswerable questions, each one darker and more oppressive than the last.

These questions—so heavy, so impossible—seem to crowd my brain all at once, leaving me feeling powerless. I can't bring myself to resolve them. Perhaps it's not for me to settle such things. Perhaps they are meant to remain unanswered. Today we won't meet. Yesterday, when we said good-bye, the sky was already changing. Clouds began to gather on the horizon, and a thin mist rose, veiling the city in a gray haze.

I remember mentioning it as we parted, almost as if I could predict what was coming. Tomorrow will be a bad day, I had said. But she said nothing in return, refusing to acknowledge even the possibility of rain. For her, the world was too bright, too full of happiness to imagine otherwise. If it rains, we won't see each other, she had said simply. I won't come. I wanted to believe she wouldn't notice the rain today, that her happiness would overpower any storm.

But she hasn't come. Yesterday was our third meeting, our third white night, a night so pure and fleeting, glowing with a light that seemed to promise eternity. And yet, here I am, alone. How radiant joy and happiness make a person, how it fills every corner of their being. Her heart was brimming yesterday, overflowing with love and excitement. You could see it in her every word, every gesture, every glance.

It was as if she wanted the whole world to share in her joy, to bask in her happiness. There was a warmth in her voice, a tenderness in her words that made me feel as though they were meant just for me. How solicitous, how kind she was yesterday. How she tried so earnestly to encourage me, to lift my spirits. Oh, the irresistible coquetry of happiness. How easily it deceives.

While she laughed and spoke with such tenderness, I—I believed it all. I thought it was real, that it came from her heart, and that it was meant for me. But my God, how could I have been so blind? How could I have fooled myself so completely? How could I not have seen that everything I thought was mine—her kindness, her smiles, her gentle words—belonged to another? None of it was truly mine.

Even her tenderness towards me, her attentiveness, her affectionate concern—yes, even what I dared to think of as her love for me was nothing but an extension of her own joy, a joy that didn't originate from me, but from the thought of seeing someone else. I was nothing more than a bystander to her happiness, a piece of her world that she wished to include in her glowing anticipation of someone else.

When he didn't come, when her hopes went unanswered, I saw her falter. The lightness in her step, the gaiety in her words—it all began to fade. Her laughter grew quieter, her movements more hesitant. And yet, strangely, she turned her attentiveness back to me, almost as if by instinct. It was as though, in the absence of her own happiness, she was trying to pass it on to me, to share what little she could still muster.

I saw then how deeply she was affected. My Nastenka—yes, I still dared to think of her as mine—was disheartened, dismayed, perhaps even heartbroken. I think in that moment she realized the truth—that I loved her. She saw my poor unspoken love reflected in my silence and in my eyes, and she felt sorry for me. When we are unhappy, it's as though we become more attuned to the suffering of others, as though our own pain sharpens our ability to recognize it.

Instead of destroying our capacity to feel, sadness concentrates it, heightens it. She must have felt my sorrow, even as she wrestled with her own. I had gone to meet her with a full heart, carrying with me all the anticipation and impatience of someone who has allowed himself to hope. I had no idea then that it would end this way, that my hopes would crumble so completely. When I arrived, she was already there, waiting for me.

She looked radiant, her face aglow with pleasure. She was expecting something—no, someone. She was expecting an answer, and that answer was him. She had arrived long before I did, her excitement so great that she couldn't wait. At first she was giddy, laughing at everything I said, even when it wasn't meant to be funny. Her laughter was infectious, but it didn't take long for me to sense the undercurrent of tension beneath it.

I tried to talk to keep the conversation light, but soon I fell silent, unable to match her mood. I was too aware of the truth that she couldn't yet admit to herself. Do you know why I'm so happy today? she asked suddenly, her eyes sparkling as she turned to me. Do you know why I like looking at you so much right now? Why? I asked, trying to keep my voice steady, though my heart was already pounding in my chest.

I like you, she said with a warm smile, because you haven't fallen in love with me. You know, in your place most men would have been sighing endlessly, pestering me with their feelings, making themselves miserable and me uncomfortable. But you, you're different. You're so nice about everything. She laughed softly, but before I could respond, she reached out and wrung my hand with such unexpected force that I almost cried out in surprise.

Her laughter grew brighter at my startled expression, and for a moment her mood seemed to lift entirely. Goodness, what a friend you are, she said, her tone shifting into something more serious, even tender as her laughter subsided. She gazed at me intently, and after a pause she added, truly, God sent you to me. I don't know what I would have done without you, especially now. What would have happened to me if you hadn't been here?

You are so unselfish, so kind, so understanding. How could anyone be more genuinely caring than you? When I am married, you and I will be the best of friends, closer than brother and sister. I shall care for you almost as much as I do for him. Her words pierced my heart. In that moment a wave of profound sadness swept over me, though I felt something else too, an inexplicable urge to laugh.

Perhaps it was the absurdity of the situation, the strange mingling of my love for her, and the knowledge that she would never return it. You're very upset right now, I said gently, trying to steady my voice. You're frightened, aren't you? You're afraid he won't come. Oh, how unkind you are, she exclaimed, though there was no anger in her tone, only a kind of playful reproach. If I were less happy, I believe I would cry at your lack of faith, at your doubts about him, and at the way you're scolding me now.

But no, I won't cry. You've made me think, though. Yes, you've given me a great deal to think about, but not now, later. For now, I must admit, you're right. She sighed, her expression softening. Yes, I am not myself right now. I feel as though I'm floating, as though everything is unreal. My nerves are all on edge, and I can't seem to feel things as deeply as I should.

Everything feels too light, too fragile. But enough about feelings, she said suddenly, cutting herself off. Let's not dwell on that. At that exact moment we heard footsteps approaching. The sound echoed faintly in the stillness of the night, growing louder as the figure drew closer. In the dim light we saw a form coming toward us. We both froze. She gasped softly, almost crying out, and I instinctively let go of her hand and took a step back, ready to walk away.

But the figure passed by without stopping. It wasn't him. What are you afraid of? Why did you let go of my hand, she asked, turning to me with a puzzled expression. Without waiting for an answer, she reached out and placed her hand in mine again. Come, it's nothing. Let's wait together. When he comes, I want him to see how fond we are of each other. How fond we are of each other, I repeated, unable to hide the bitterness in my voice.

Inside my heart ached as I thought, oh Nastenka, Nastenka, how much you've just revealed to me with those words. Such fondness in moments like this makes the heart grow cold and the soul unbearably heavy. Your hand is cold in mine, while mine burns like fire. How blind you are, Nastenka, to the truth right in front of you. Oh, how unbearable a happy person can be sometimes, and yet how could I ever be angry with you?

The emotion swirling within me grew too intense to contain. At last my heart overflowed. Listen, Nastenka, I burst out. Do you have any idea how my day has been? Do you know what I've been feeling all this time? She looked at me with wide eyes, a mixture of curiosity and concern. What do you mean? How has your day been? Tell me. Tell me quickly. Why haven't you said anything until now?

Well, I began struggling to find the right words. To start with, after I carried out all your commissions, delivering the letter, visiting your kind friends, then—then I went home and went straight to bed. Is that all? she interrupted, breaking into laughter. Yes, almost all, I answered, trying to hold myself together as foolish, inexplicable tears threatened to well up in my eyes. I woke up an hour before our appointment, though, truth be told.

It felt as though I hadn't slept at all. I can't explain it. I don't even know what happened to me. It was as if time had stopped entirely, as though the world itself had paused in that one fleeting moment. I came here to tell you everything, Nastenka, feeling like that single sensation, that single overwhelming feeling, had taken hold of me forever. It was as if one minute of my life had stretched out endlessly, as though it could last for all eternity, and everything else—the entire world—had come to a halt.

When I woke, it was as if some old forgotten melody, one I had once known so well long ago, but had since lost in the recesses of memory, had returned to me. It was a tune so sweet, so achingly familiar, that it seemed to echo deep in my heart. And I felt as though that melody had been waiting there all along, knocking at my soul, yearning to be heard.

And now, at last, it had broken through. Oh, my goodness, my goodness! Nastenka interrupted, her voice cutting through my reverie. What on earth are you talking about? I don't understand a word of it! Her bluntness startled me, and I faltered, my hopes dimming. Yet there was still a faint, lingering hope hidden in my voice as I tried to explain. Ah, Nastenka, I said plaintively, I was just trying to describe to you that strange, overwhelming impression.

Stop it, hush! she said suddenly, and in an instant I could see that she had guessed. Her sharp intuition had uncovered what I hadn't dared to say outright. Her mood shifted abruptly. With a mischievous smile, she became extraordinarily lively, talkative, and playful. She slipped her arm through mine, laughing with a lightness that seemed almost calculated. Every faltering, confused word I tried to speak only made her laugh more, her laughter bright and ringing.

Her amusement, so sudden and unrelenting, began to irritate me. It felt as though she was flirting deliberately, as though she was trying to mask or deflect something deeper. Do you know, she began suddenly, still laughing, I feel a little offended that you aren't in love with me? Isn't that strange? How contradictory human nature is! But then again, Mr. Unapproachable, she added teasingly, you can't blame me for being so simple.

I tell you everything, every silly, foolish thought that pops into my head. It's just who I am. Her words stung, though I tried not to show it. I glanced away, searching for a distraction. Listen, I said, catching the faint sound of a bell ringing in the distance. That must be eleven o'clock. The slow, deliberate chimes echoed faintly through the quiet night. She stopped suddenly, her laughter fading as her expression changed.

She stood still, her face tense, and began counting the strokes. I regretted saying it immediately. The look of nervous uncertainty in her eyes, the way her voice trembled as she whispered, yes, it's eleven, filled me with a sharp pang of guilt. Why had I done that? Why had I deliberately reminded her of the time? I cursed myself for my petty impulse, for the spiteful satisfaction I had felt just a moment ago.

She was anxious enough already, and now I had made it worse. I wanted to take it back, to undo the fear and sadness I had just caused. Now, Nastenka, I said softly, trying to comfort her, don't worry, please, let's think this through rationally. There's no reason to believe the worst yet. There are so many possible explanations for why he hasn't come. Let me explain, and you'll see it's not as bad as it seems.

She looked at me, her eyes wide and searching, desperate for reassurance. I knew she wanted to believe me, to hold on to hope, and it gave me the strength to press on. Look, I began, my voice growing steadier as I warmed to my task. It's entirely possible that he hasn't received your letter yet. Think about it, what if he wasn't at home when it arrived? He might not have read it, even now, or perhaps he read it but wasn't able to respond immediately.

There are so many reasons why he might not be here yet. Suppose he's planning to answer the letter but couldn't come until tomorrow. Anything could have delayed him. As I spoke, I could see her tension easing, her breathing slowing. She wanted so much to believe me, and I wanted even more to make her believe, to ease her worry even for a little while. At that moment she was so vulnerable, so ready to grasp at any straw of hope.

I continued, feeling a strange sense of responsibility, almost a duty to shield her from despair. I'll tell you what, I said finally, feeling more confident now. As soon as it's light tomorrow, I'll go to check for his reply myself. If there's an answer, I'll bring it to you immediately. We'll know for sure then. But until that happens, don't let yourself think the worst. There are thousands of possibilities.

Anything could have happened. She nodded slowly, her face softening as the faintest flicker of hope returned to her eyes. For a moment it seemed as though she had found a little peace. Yes, yes, said Nastenka eagerly, as though suddenly awakened to a new possibility. I didn't think of that. Of course anything could happen, she added, though her voice trailed off into a tone of quiet resignation. There was no real conviction behind her words, only a faint, distant echo of another thought, some vexing discord lingering in her mind, unresolved.

I know what you must do, she said after a pause, her tone growing more certain. Go as early as you can tomorrow morning, the very first thing. If you hear anything, anything at all, let me know immediately. You know where I live, don't you? She began to repeat her address to me, her voice hurried and yet soft, as though she needed to make sure I would remember every word.

Her insistence made me feel a strange pang of sadness, a deep longing to reassure her, to promise her more than I could. Then quite suddenly her mood shifted, she became unusually tender, almost maternal in the way she looked at me, her concern for me clear in every glance, every movement. She listened attentively as I spoke, nodding slightly as though she wanted me to believe she was truly hearing me.

Yet when I asked her a question, she faltered, her silence spoke louder than any words might have. Her confusion deepened and she turned her head away, unable to meet my eyes. I leaned in slightly, trying to understand what was happening. When she finally turned back toward me, I saw it, tears glistening in her eyes. She was crying, though she was trying desperately to hide it. Nastenka, I said softly, alarmed by her sudden shift.

How can you? Why are you crying? Oh, what a child you are! What childishness! Come now, don't cry. Please don't. She tried to smile through her tears, brushing them away quickly as though embarrassed by her display of emotion. It's nothing, she murmured, though her chin quivered and her chest still heaved with the effort to compose herself, she was fighting to steady her breathing, to regain her usual cheerfulness.

But the struggle was written all over her face. After a moment of silence, she spoke again, her voice softer, more contemplative. I was thinking about you, she said, almost to herself. You're so kind, you're so good. I would have to be made of stone not to feel it. Do you know what I was just thinking? I was comparing you two. She hesitated, then looked directly at me, her eyes filled with strange mixture of sadness and warmth.

Why isn't he you? Why isn't he like you? You are so much better than he is. He isn't half as kind, half as thoughtful. And yet—yet I love him more than I could ever love you. Her words pierced through me, leaving me speechless. I couldn't summon a single response. I didn't know what to say, and for a moment neither did she. She seemed to expect something, though, a word, a look, anything.

But I stayed silent, struggling to contain the storm of emotions her confession had unleashed within me. Perhaps, she said after another long pause, as though trying to fill the silence herself, perhaps it's just that I don't understand him fully yet. You know, I've always been a little afraid of him. He's so serious, so proud. At least that's how he seems. But I know it's only a facade, deep down I know there's more tenderness in his heart than even in mine.

I remember how he looked at me that day, when I went to him with my little bundle. Do you remember? I told you about it. He seemed so kind, so sad. And yet—I feel like I respect him too much. Doesn't that prove that we aren't equals? No, Nastenka, I replied gently, my voice barely above a whisper. It doesn't prove that you aren't equals. It proves that you love him more than anything in the world.

More than yourself, even. She looked at me with wide, thoughtful eyes, as though my words had struck a chord deep within her. Yes, she said at last, her voice tinged with naive sincerity. Yes, maybe you're right, but do you know what strikes me now? She paused, her tone growing more reflective. I'm not talking about him anymore, not about anyone in particular, just speaking generally. This is something I've thought about before.

Why can't we all just be like brothers to one another? Why is it that even the best people seem to hide parts of themselves from others, as if they're keeping something back? Why can't we simply say what's in our hearts, openly and honestly, especially when we know our words won't be empty or meaningless? Instead, we put up walls, we act distant, and we make ourselves seem harsher than we really are.

It's as if everyone is afraid to show their feelings, afraid to express them too quickly, as though they might somehow cheapen them by doing so. Oh, Nastenka, I said, my heart aching at her words. What you're saying is true, painfully true, but there are so many reasons for it, so many complicated reasons. Even as I spoke, I felt myself suppressing my own feelings more than ever, struggling to keep my voice calm, to conceal the turmoil raging within me.

No, no, she said suddenly, her voice charged with deep emotion. You, for instance, you're not like other people. I don't even know how to explain what I mean. She hesitated, her words faltering as though she was trying to grasp something intangible. It's hard for me to put it into words, but it seems to me that you, right now, at this very moment, it seems to me that you're sacrificing something for me.

Her voice softened as she added this, and she glanced at me briefly, almost shyly, as if afraid of my reaction. Forgive me for saying so, she went on timidly, her voice trembling as she tried to keep her composure. I'm just a simple girl, I've seen so little of life, and sometimes I feel like I don't even know how to say what I want to say. She smiled faintly, but there was a quiver in her lips, as though she was holding back something deeper, something she couldn't quite articulate.

I only wanted to tell you that I'm grateful. I feel it, deeply. Oh, may God bless you for it. May He grant you happiness, more than you can imagine. Her words were like a balm and a wound at the same time. She spoke with such sincerity that it was impossible to feel bitterness, even as her meaning pierced me. What you told me about your dreamer, she continued, is not true anymore.

Not about you, at least. You've changed, you've recovered. You're not the same man you described to me. She looked at me with something like pride, as though she were acknowledging a transformation she herself had brought about. If you ever fall in love with someone, really fall in love, I pray that God grants you happiness with her. I don't need to wish anything for her, though, because she will be happy.

I know it. I'm a woman, after all, and I understand these things. Believe me when I tell you this. She fell silent then, her words hanging in the air between us, and for a moment neither of us could speak. She pressed my hand warmly, her grip firm yet tender, as though she wanted to convey everything she couldn't put into words through that single gesture. I felt my throat tighten with emotion, but I couldn't bring myself to respond.

The weight of her words, their bittersweet kindness, held me silent. Minutes passed in this quiet shared understanding. At last she lifted her head and broke the silence. It's clear he won't come tonight, she said softly, her voice steady but tinged with resignation. It's late now. I forced myself to reply, summoning all the conviction I could muster. He'll come tomorrow, I said firmly, as though by sheer will I could make it true.

Yes, she said after a pause, and this time there was no trace of her earlier doubt. Her voice was calm, almost cheerful. I see now that it's impossible for him to come before tomorrow. Well, good-bye then, till tomorrow. If it rains I might not come, but the day after tomorrow I'll come for certain. Whatever happens, I'll be here. Promise me you'll come too. I need to see you.

I'll tell you everything. As we parted she gave me her hand again, this time holding it longer, as though she was reluctant to let go. Her eyes met mine with a rare openness, a kind of pure sincerity that took my breath away. We'll always be together, won't we? she asked candidly, her voice filled with quiet hope. Oh, Nastenka, Nastenka, if only you knew how lonely I am now.

When nine o'clock struck that evening I couldn't bear to stay indoors. The hours seemed to stretch endlessly, and the walls of my room felt like they were closing in around me. I put on my coat and stepped outside, indifferent to the damp chill of the weather. The rain had eased, but the streets were still slick and gleaming under the faint glow of the streetlights. I walked without direction, my feet carrying me almost instinctively to the embankment.

There I sat on the bench we had shared, staring out into the dark, restless waters. After a while I found myself walking toward her street. My heart beat faster with every step, a strange mix of anticipation and dread building within me. But when I was only a few steps away from her door, I stopped. Shame washed over me like a cold wave. What was I doing? I couldn't bring myself to look at her windows.

I turned abruptly and walked away, my shoulders hunched against the damp air, my thoughts heavier than ever. I returned home feeling more dejected than I had ever been before. The dreary day seemed to reflect my own desolation, each raindrop a small echo of the ache in my heart. If the weather had been fine, perhaps I would have wandered the streets all night trying to escape my thoughts, but the rain drove me back, forcing me to sit with my loneliness.

Still I clung to the promise of tomorrow. Tomorrow she would come, and she would tell me everything. Tomorrow would bring answers, resolution, perhaps even hope. The letter hadn't arrived yet, of course, but I told myself that was to be expected. By now, I thought bitterly, they must already be together.

My God, how has it all ended? What has it all come to? I arrived promptly at nine o'clock, my heart heavy with foreboding. From a distance I saw her already there, standing as she had stood that first evening, her elbows resting on the railing, gazing out over the canal. She was so still, so lost in thought, that she didn't hear my footsteps approaching. ''Nastenka!'' I called softly, suppressing the tremor in my voice with all the strength I could muster.

She turned quickly, her face alight with anxious expectation. ''Well?'' she said urgently. ''Well? Make haste!'' Her voice was tense, as if she couldn't bear another second of uncertainty. I hesitated for a moment, unsure how to begin. Her eyes searched mine, brimming with hope and fear. ''Well, where is the letter? Have you brought the letter?'' she demanded, clutching at the cold metal of the railing as though it might steady her.

I felt my throat tighten as I answered, my voice low and strained. ''No, there is no letter,'' I said at last. ''Hasn't he been to you yet?'' As soon as the words left my mouth, I saw the colour drain from her face. She turned so pale, so ghostly, that I thought she might collapse right there before me, her wide, unblinking eyes locked on mine, and she stared at me as if I had just struck the final blow to her fragile hope.

I had shattered her last dream, the thread of possibility she'd been clinging to with all her strength. ''Well?'' she said finally, her voice breaking as though each word cost her unimaginable effort. ''God be with him. God be with him, if he leaves me like that.'' Her head dropped, and her gaze fell to the ground. She seemed unable to look at me, as though the weight of her humiliation was too great to bear.

For several agonizing moments she fought with her emotions, her body trembling with the effort to hold herself together. Then all at once she turned away. Leaning her elbows against the railing again, she buried her face in her hands and broke into heart-wrenching sobs. ''Oh, don't! Don't!'' I began, stepping toward her. But as I looked at her crumpled figure, I felt my words falter. What could I say to her?

How could I possibly console her when her pain was so raw, so absolute? ''Don't try to comfort me,'' she said through her tears, her voice trembling yet resolute. ''Don't talk about him. Don't tell me that he'll come, that he hasn't abandoned me so cruelly and inhumanly. What's the point? What's the point of false hope?'' She paused, struggling to steady her voice, but her sobs rose again, choking her words.

''Can it be—can it be that there was something in my letter? Something wrong? Something—unlucky?'' She couldn't go on. Her sobs overwhelmed her once more, and my heart ached as I watched her shoulders shake with despair. ''Oh, how cruelly! How inhumanly cruel this is!'' she cried out after a moment.
